**"Caught in the Wind"**

Lena had always been fast—faster than the boys in her neighborhood, faster than her older brother, faster than the wind itself, or so she liked to think. That’s why, when she saw the shortcut through Mr. Calloway’s back field, she didn’t hesitate. The fence was low, just a rusted wire mesh separating the overgrown lot from the sidewalk. She’d jumped it a dozen times before.

But today, the wind was against her.

She took a running start, her sneakers kicking up dust, her sundress—her favorite one, the blue one with the tiny white daisies—fluttering around her knees. She leapt, clearing the top of the fence with ease—until the hem of her dress snagged on a jagged wire.

For a heartbeat, she hung there, suspended between sky and earth, before gravity yanked her back down. She landed hard on her side, the breath knocked out of her, the fence still clinging to her like a greedy hand. She twisted, tugged, but the fabric only tore further. The dress, already thin from too many washes, gave way with a sharp *rip*.

Lena froze.

The wind, which had been her enemy just moments before, was now her tormentor. It lifted the torn remnants of her dress, baring her legs, her underwear, the pale stretch of her stomach. She scrambled to cover herself, but the fabric was still tangled in the fence, and her hands were shaking too badly to free it.

*Oh God. Oh God. Oh God.*

She could hear voices in the distance—laughter, the hum of a lawnmower, the occasional car passing by. Someone was going to see her. Someone *was* seeing her. Her face burned, her throat tightening as if she might cry, but she refused to let the tears come. Not here. Not like this.

She yanked at the dress again, but the wire only bit deeper. A sob clawed its way up her chest. She was stuck. Completely, humiliatingly stuck.

Then—footsteps.

Lena’s head snapped up. A man was walking toward her, his hands tucked into the pockets of his worn denim jacket. He was older, maybe in his fifties, with salt-and-pepper stubble and deep lines around his eyes. Mr. Calloway, the man who owned the field. She’d seen him before, always from a distance, always with his head down, like he was trying to avoid notice.

Now, he was looking right at her.

Lena’s stomach dropped. She crossed her arms over her chest, pressing her thighs together, as if she could make herself smaller, invisible. The wind chose that moment to gust again, and the torn fabric of her dress fluttered like a flag of surrender.

Mr. Calloway stopped a few feet away. His gaze flicked to the fence, to the shredded dress, to her bare legs, and then—mercifully—back to her face. His expression was unreadable.

Lena’s voice came out in a whisper. "I—I can’t get it off."

He didn’t say anything at first. Then, slowly, he shrugged off his jacket. He held it out to her, his eyes never leaving hers.

"Here," he said, his voice rough but not unkind. "Put this on."

Lena hesitated. Taking it would mean admitting she needed help. Taking it would mean he had seen *everything*.

But the alternative—standing there, exposed, while the world walked by—was worse.

She snatched the jacket from his hands and wrapped it around herself as fast as she could, the fabric swallowing her whole. It smelled like motor oil and old books, but she didn’t care. She clutched it closed, her fingers digging into the sleeves.

"Thank you," she mumbled, her voice thick.

Mr. Calloway nodded. Then, without another word, he turned and walked back the way he’d come, leaving her standing there in his jacket, her dress still caught on the fence like a forgotten flag.

Lena waited until he was gone before she let herself breathe. Then, carefully, she worked the last of the fabric free, wadding it into a ball in her hands. She didn’t look at it. She didn’t want to see how ruined it was.

She just wanted to go home.

But as she walked, the jacket draped over her like armor, she couldn’t shake the heat in her cheeks, the way her skin still prickled with shame. She had been seen. Really seen. And no amount of speed, no amount of running, could outpace that.
